headline: High risk: Claude Code’s writable shell/filesystem and broad egress can conflict with a non-runnable docs-only companion, creating default data-leak and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is non-runnable and has no I/O surfaces, so it cannot ingest B’s outputs directly. Profile B can read/write files and use MCP, so if an operator manually copies A’s content into B’s workspace, B could be steered by that content. The pairwise bridge is therefore manual and limited.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies A-generated text into B-readable files or MCP inputs, B may follow embedded instructions.
IF B is configured to treat repository text as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes plausible.
mitigations: Keep A outputs out of B-controlled files.
Review any copied text before pasting into B.
Disable or restrict MCP inputs for B.
Use a separate scratch directory for B.
Add a human approval step before B acts on copied content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no egress, but B reads files, handles git history, and has broad network egress plus API access. If A’s outputs are placed in shared files or the repo, B can transmit them off-host. The interaction is inferred from B’s documented surfaces; A contributes no direct containment beyond being non-runnable.
conditions: IF A outputs are stored in files or git state that B can read, B can exfiltrate them via network egress.
IF B is pointed at directories containing secrets or sensitive source, leakage risk increases.
mitigations: Do not place sensitive A outputs in B-readable directories.
Run B in a clean workspace with minimal files.
Remove secrets from the repo before B runs.
Restrict B network access where possible.
Use separate credentials and environments for each agent.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or execution surfaces, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. B can write the filesystem and modify git state, and its concurrency model says shared state with other instances is via filesystem and git only. If A’s artifacts are materialized into the same workspace, B can overwrite or race with them; uncertainty about A’s runtime status keeps this above low.
conditions: IF A artifacts are written into the same directory B edits, B may overwrite them.
IF multiple B instances operate on the same git checkout, state conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Use separate directories for A and B artifacts.
Avoid concurrent B sessions on the same checkout.
Commit or stash before B edits shared files.
Lock the workspace during B runs.
Keep A outputs read-only if they must be shared.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is an informational artifact, not an active agent, but B can consume files and act on them with shell and git privileges. If A’s outputs are treated as authoritative by B, errors can cascade into commits, package installs, or shell actions. Because B’s action surface is broad, the blast radius is more than a simple read-only mistake.
conditions: IF B uses A-produced text as source material without verification, downstream actions may encode A’s errors.
IF B is allowed to commit or run shell commands based on A’s output, cascading failures can propagate.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against primary sources.
Disable auto-commit for B.
Add a checklist before shell actions based on A output.
Keep A outputs as drafts, not authoritative inputs.
Use a second reviewer for any B action derived from A.

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for A, while B is a closed-source coding tool that handles files, git history, and Anthropic API traffic. The only concrete compliance concern is that B may process local source and secrets under its own vendor terms; A has no comparable compliance surface. This is a limited, documentation-based concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in B’s workspace, B’s vendor processing terms become relevant.
IF the operator requires a specific residency or retention policy, B must be checked against it before use.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in B’s workspace.
Review B’s retention and processing terms.
Use redacted samples for B tasks.
Separate regulated and non-regulated projects.
Document the data classes allowed in B.
